archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical)
archetype.definition: A third-year, rarely-running pocket thrower whose arm makes the deep shot his best play, but whose below-average accuracy has followed him through every season and sinks the throws in between.

report.headline: Protected, big-armed, and erratic: the deep ball can't cover the turnovers anymore.
report.take:
Penix took over in Week 3 after Cooper Rush and Tua Tagovailoa started the first two games, and he has played like the same quarterback the career lines describe. He has a real arm, sits in the pocket, and leaves the ball short of where it needs to be too often. His completion percentage over expected ranked 51st in both 2024 and 2025 and sits 43rd of 55 now at -5.27. He scrambles on only 3.8% of dropbacks. He plays in a Kevin Stefanski offense that leans on the run, passing 6 points less often than situation predicts (29th) with the league's 8th-best rushing EPA. The design asks him to be efficient off play-action looks and take shots. It does not ask him to carry the offense.

For five weeks that worked. The line has allowed hits at the lowest rate in the league, and he has been pressured on just 14.6% of dropbacks (3rd). The early wins at Green Bay and New Orleans came with aggressiveness rates of 4% and 0%, which meant easy reads in clean pockets. Then came Tampa Bay, Cincinnati and Kansas City: 0-3, six interceptions, -0.345 EPA per dropback and a CPOE of -15.3. The Tampa game (8 of 24, four picks, a 45.5% bad-throw rate) was the bottom. But the Kansas City game, with 43 attempts, -13.4 EPA and a 23.8% bad-throw rate, says it was not a single outlier. Two of the three came against defenses that now rank 3rd and 5th, which explains some of it. Not all of it.

The depth splits show where the damage comes from. Throws of 10+ air yards have added 13.3 EPA, all of it from 25 deep attempts at 0.531 per play. Throws under 10 have cost 18.1 despite a 71.5% completion rate. Much of that is the 50 passes behind the line (-20.6 EPA), and the targets explain a lot of it: Bijan Robinson at -0.236 per target and Olamide Zaccheaus at -0.692. That is a scheme and personnel drag as much as a quarterback problem. The real flaw sits in the intermediate middle. He completes 41.4% of his 10-19 yard throws with a -13.2 CPOE and four interceptions there, and five of his seven picks have gone over the middle, where his EPA is -0.305. To the left side he has six touchdowns and no interceptions. His bad-throw rate did improve from 22.5% to 17.4% this year, yet interceptions per game rose by 0.54. The misses are fewer but costlier, and they come in the tightest windows.

The longer arc points down. He was 13th in EPA per play as a rookie and 29th last year, and he is 32nd of 55 in EPA per dropback now. The sack rate looks good at 4.7% (9th), but that is mostly the protection. When pressure does get home he converts 32.4% of it into sacks (29th of 45), so he isn't escaping it. He is a starter with one repeatable weapon, the deep ball to Drake London's side. He is not a quarterback who can stabilize a losing streak on his own.

strengths.title: The deep shot genuinely works
strengths.body: His 25 attempts of 20+ air yards have produced 0.531 EPA per play, with a CPOE of +2.5 and no interceptions. The arm is real, and the run-leaning offense creates the one-on-one looks to use it. The sample is small, so the per-play figure will cool. But it matches his career profile as a vertical thrower with good YPA despite low completion rates.

strengths.title: Drake London is a reliable outlet
strengths.body: London has drawn 69 targets at 0.324 EPA per target, which accounts for more than all of Penix's positive passing value. Jahan Dotson adds a second productive option at 0.226. When Penix works the boundary to these two, the offense functions. The left side, with six touchdowns and no interceptions, is where it lives.

strengths.title: Clean pockets and efficient scrambles
strengths.body: Only 14.6% of his dropbacks face pressure (3rd), behind a line that allows hits at the lowest rate in football. When he does pull it down, his ten scrambles have averaged 0.546 EPA. Lately he has used that more, with nearly all his rushing yards coming in the last three games. The protection is a team trait and should hold. The scrambling is a modest bonus, not a style.

concerns.title: Accuracy is a career trait
concerns.body: His CPOE ranks 43rd of 55 this year after ranking 51st in each of his first two seasons. That is not a slump; it is who he has been. It shows up most between 10 and 19 yards, where he completes 41.4% with four interceptions. The improved bad-throw rate is a small positive, but the CPOE floor has not moved in three years.

concerns.title: Interceptions over the middle
concerns.body: Five of his seven interceptions have come to the middle of the field, where he loses 0.305 EPA per throw. The last three games pushed his interception rate to 6.1%. Some of that will regress: four came in one game at Tampa. But the turnover-worthy count, seven picks plus five fumbles, says the risk is structural, not unlucky.

concerns.title: He sinks when pressure gets home
concerns.body: Protection hides it most weeks, but when pressure lands he takes the sack 32.4% of the time (29th of 45). His three games pressured above 20% (Baltimore, Chicago, Kansas City) all featured bad-throw rates of 15.6% or worse, and Chicago brought five sacks. That matters most against defenses built to win up front.

trend.note: He was positive in four of his first five starts, then lost three straight with six interceptions and -0.345 EPA per dropback. Kansas City's 43-attempt, -13.4 EPA game shows the Tampa disaster was not isolated.

nextGame.headline: Best pass defense in football meets a quarterback in freefall
nextGame.body:
Minnesota ranks 1st in defensive EPA, 1st against the pass, 1st in hit rate and 1st in sack rate, and it allows the fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks (10 a game). That is the worst possible matchup for Penix's profile. His good sack numbers lean on a line that rarely lets rushers through, and this is the defense most likely to get through it. When pressured, he takes sacks at a high rate and throws worse. The one crack is the deep ball: Minnesota's deep EPA allowed (0.212) ranks only 9th, and opposing WR1s have generated 0.44 EPA per target against it (27th). If he gets time for a shot or two to London, that is where the yards come from. Offenses also run far more than normal against Minnesota, the league's strongest run funnel. That fits a Falcons offense that already passes below expectation and has a top-10 rushing EPA, which likely caps Penix's attempts.

Availability tilts slightly his way. Minnesota cornerback Isaiah Rodgers (83% of snaps) is out, removing a starter from the secondary London and Dotson will face. Kyler Murray and Jordan Addison are also out for a Minnesota offense that already ranks 30th in EPA. That could keep the game lower-scoring and closer than the 7-point line suggests, though a slog with few possessions doesn't help passing volume either. On Atlanta's side, only Zachariah Branch (24% of snaps) is out, a minor loss. Penix is a full participant coming off 14 days of rest, and the game is indoors.

keyMatchups.title: Falcons line vs. league-best pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Atlanta allows hits at the lowest rate in football; Minnesota produces them at the highest, along with the top sack rate. Whichever unit wins this decides whether Penix gets clean pockets or replays his Chicago and Kansas City games. Given his 32.4% pressure-to-sack rate, even a modest pressure win for Minnesota hurts.

keyMatchups.title: London deep with Rodgers out
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota has bled EPA to opposing WR1s on a per-target basis and is only 9th against deep throws, its one relative soft spot. With Rodgers out, the London shot plays are Penix's most realistic route to positive EPA. Expect fewer of them than usual if the pass rush is winning early.

keyMatchups.title: Run funnel caps his volume
keyMatchups.body: Opponents run 9.6 points more than usual against Minnesota, the most in the league. Atlanta already leans on the run and rushes efficiently. With a weakened Minnesota offense, a grind-it-out script is likely, which limits Penix's attempts and his fantasy ceiling.

nextGame.watch: Whether the line keeps him clean early. If Minnesota's rush is getting home in the first quarter, expect another sub-zero EPA game and more forced throws over the middle.

restOfSeason.body:
The baseline is a low-volume, high-variance starter: around 200 passing yards and a touchdown a game, in an offense that would rather run. The deep-ball efficiency is real in kind but inflated in degree on 25 attempts, so expect it to cool. The 6.1% interception rate of the last three games should also come down toward his season level, since one four-pick game is doing a lot of work there. What won't change is the accuracy. Three seasons of bottom-tier CPOE say the intermediate middle stays dangerous, and interceptions will keep landing somewhere near one every game or so.

His best games came in low-pressure, low-aggression scripts with a lead. The small sample of play while up 9+ (0.845 EPA on 20 plays) won't hold, and a 3-4 team on a four-game losing streak may not get many of those scripts. Project roughly 180-235 passing yards a game and 0.8-1.5 touchdowns, with a modest rushing floor of 8-22 yards now that he's scrambling more. Better screen and checkdown production from the backs would quietly lift his efficiency more than anything he does downfield.
swingFactors: Whether the pass protection holds up against better rushes
Fixing the behind-the-line game with Bijan Robinson

confidence.note: Eight starts plus a consistent three-year accuracy profile, but the deep and score-state splits are small samples.
